record.paper_title: Quantum Communication: From Fundamentals to Recent Trends, Challenges and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can quantum internet end devices reliably store quantum-state information after entanglement is established while preserving the coherence of memory qubits during operations on other qubits within the same node?

evidence.quote: End Devices: The first major requirement for the end nodes is to reliably store quantum state information when the entanglement is set up.
The major challenge of extending these point-to-point entangled links to an actual quantum network, as pointed out in [197], is the reliable storage of the quantum states in the nodes.
there are scenarios where unwanted couplings can significantly impact the coherence of a memory qubit during operations on another qubit within the same node [205], [206].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum network in which spatially separated end nodes share entangled pairs of qubits. Each end node contains a multi-qubit register: some qubits are designated as "memory qubits" that store quantum states (e.g., halves of established entangled pairs), while other qubits in the same node are used for ongoing operations such as gate execution, measurement, or fresh entanglement generation with neighboring nodes. Memory qubits suffer decoherence due to coupling with the environment and, crucially, due to unwanted couplings to other qubits in the same node when those qubits are being manipulated.

Develop a protocol and/or physical architecture for the end nodes that simultaneously achieves the following:

1. After an entangled pair is established between two end nodes, the memory qubit at each node faithfully retains its quantum state (i.e., preserves entanglement with the remote partner qubit) for a duration sufficient to perform subsequent network-level tasks such as entanglement swapping or distillation.

2. While the memory qubit is storing this state, arbitrary local quantum operations (single- and two-qubit gates, measurements, and re-initialization) may be carried out on other qubits residing in the same node without degrading the coherence of, or causing measurable disturbance to, the memory qubit beyond a specified tolerance.

Quantify, in terms of a chosen figure of merit (for example, the average fidelity F(t) between the stored state and its ideal counterpart, or the entanglement fidelity with the remote qubit), the achievable trade-off between memory storage time, the number and type of operations that can be applied to neighboring qubits during storage, and the strength of the unwanted intra-node couplings. Provide bounds, constructions, or impossibility results that characterize when reliable memory-plus-operation coexistence is feasible.
artifact.status_search_result: Reliable long-lived quantum memory coexisting with operations on other qubits within the same node is widely identified as an unresolved engineering and physics challenge for the quantum internet. While significant experimental progress (e.g., NV-center registers with nuclear-spin memories, trapped ions, and neutral atom arrays) has extended coherence times and demonstrated partial isolation, no general solution that fully preserves memory-qubit coherence during arbitrary operations on co-located qubits has been established. The problem remains an active area of research.

status_evidence.title: Realization of a multinode quantum network of remote solid-state qubits
status_evidence.snippet: Demonstrates a three-node network using NV centers with nuclear-spin memory qubits, while noting limitations on memory coherence during operations on the electron spin.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art demonstrations still face memory decoherence induced by operations on neighboring qubits within the same node.

status_evidence.title: Quantum internet: A vision for the road ahead
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies reliable quantum memory at end nodes as a key open requirement for building a functional quantum internet.
status_evidence.claim: Reliable end-node quantum memory is listed as an open requirement.
